title: Andrew Doull - Roguelike Radio 2011-present
speaker: Andrew Doull
description: The history of Roguelike Radio, a podcast about roguelikes which has been running since 2011.

segments.text: ALEXEI: Welcoming to the stage Andrew Doull. Developed Unangband, an Angband
variant; wrote ASCII dreams, a roguelike developer blog; cofounded Roguelike Radio;
coined the term Procedural Content Generation; since then a board game and TTRPG designer.
Welcome all of the way from Australia I believe. ANDREW: Can you hear me? Welcome to "Roguelike
Radio 2011present." A podcast where all participants are wonderful people and go
on to have amazing lives. Kawa asked me to do a lightning talk but I am not sure what to say
so this is mostly to point out our existing body of work and it is there. I am going to
warn you as the speaker of New Zealand English I will talk about 20% faster than any human would
do. So I will get through these slides in well under 10 minutes. That's fine unless you are
the transcription teams because you are probably one of those sickos who listen to podcast at 250
speed. Today I want to talk about how this worked out from 2011 to the present day.
We begin with a question I feel like I have been forced to answer many times. Why is this a thing
that should obviously exist which is not being made? There is an Angband variant with dungeon
that feel reals. Software TTRPG using realistic rocket physics. This is an entirely selfish
project but looks impressive because it has kept going. It is just a consequence of ongoing work,
support from the community, and occasional big picture and steering oversight. Unlike many other
projects I have worked on, I have collaborated with many, Darren gray and then many who have
come on the show as Panelists and members of the broader community and volunteers. We
started auspiciously, literally. The problem being somewhere long enough is you get live through the
consequences of predictions. I want you to cast your mind back to 2011 and think about what you
were doing. I was being a fear a fulltime father father of twins. Podcasts got me through a lot of
sleepless nights. I tried to remember where you were in 2011 representing the green line.
I position this against the board of picture of roguelites. The present -day space feels
like individual developers and collaborators each working on a fantasy heartbreaker to steal a turn
from the tabletop roleplay community. Sometimes those games would get released. I released mine,
unAngband. The seven day roguelike commutation starts what I term the roguelike renaissance.
Coffee break roguelikes. There is a real story to be told here by a better scholar than me.
The Xbox 360 release of splunky to the Slay the Spire release. And then followed by roguelikes
appearing in much greater quantities on Steam. The first radio correlates with the indie scene
but is indebted to this. And finally the rogue apocalypse. Let's talk about each episode.
Episodes run slightly longer than 60 minutes and come out after being recorded and edited. We have
not had as far as I am aware anyone giving us a game for free. We have been given games.
I don't have time to list all the topics we have covered but luckily roguelikeradio.com has a list
of all prior episodes. These titles usually convey the topic being covered. Be aware the
feed has a size limit meaning the oldest episodes are not available on the feed and you have to
go to the website to get them. Managing the feed has been the most technical part of the process.
It turns out roguelikes take a lot of time to play. This is a democratizing process. We will
get a knowledgeable volunteer from the community to talk about the game occasionally. All I am
interested in when I am hosting the show is that you have something interesting to say.
That's why I choose not to introduce guests with backgrounds that may convey authority. We are all
the same symbol. We welcome English as a speech language, speech impediment, people of color
and the LGBTQIA plus community and we never get enough. Did I mention roguelikes take a lot of
time to play. We don't like the conversation topics. There is plenty of games we haven't
covered. Amega is the most egregious example. When you have a long game, people end up playing it for
a long time and know a lot about the game. There is something about repeatedly pulling an unarmed
band machine that is reflected by the real world. Games will test sets of rules. I had the pleasure
of working a libertarian who produces games under cutting this thesis framing the power
of collective action. And speaking of lies here is some statistics. I have never understood what is
suspiciously secret about these numbers but I want to put numbers out there because I believe people
should be transparent about this thing. My number one piece of advice about recording a pod cost is
if you spend money on one thing spend it on the software. You want client side. We use about 30
seconds of audio that is not in our control. You want a room that has soft furnishing. Microphones
are never an issue. We recorded five people using a headset in the middle of a wooden table. The
editor is equalizing volumes and separating talk and cleanup. I spend a lot of time removing audio
reduction and lip smacks. We manually level things now. I just wanted to pick out a few highlights.
The episode for design trying designing for visually impaired was important for me because
I have a family member who is blind and we did an episode on using a screen reader. We
listened to voice recordings and threaded into the show. Editing has been a challenge. The binding
of the episode is almost completely reiterated because I started the interview and did the intro
introduction halfway through the conversation. I really shouldn't be the person doing this. I
smack my lips and I overrun other speakers. I am not saying this in a self-deprecating manner but
because I have edited so many episodes I know where my weaknesses are. For every episode I
don't appear in is a highlight not just for me but for you the listener as well. The biggest
highlight as a community was being right. We knew there was something special about roguelikes. It
took the seven day roguelike competition and talented insiders and outsiders and a lot of
effort and discussion from people that had been around since Rogue was written. We fucking won.
Roguelikes have taken over. And we got grumpy and made slides with the word like apocalypse. We are
at the Roguelike Celebration so let's celebrate. ALEXEI: We have some time for questions
if people want to get those up. ANDREW: I have a question slide on
the wrong screen of my presentation. I am just going to see if Kawa can get through to me.
ALEXEI: It is great. We like to have lis historic talks about Roguelike Celebration because one of
the things I love about roguelikes is it holds on to its history and so much exist in a form
that can be connected. And people stay in the scene so long. We can talk to people who were
involved and Roguelike Radio has had so many guests. Giving we are living in a time when
talking about what a roguelike is has taken another turn of just like everything is a
roguelike now. It felt like a good time to do a retrospective so Thank you for taking on the task.
ALEXEI: Thank you for inviting me and forcing me to do this. I realize I had gone even faster
than I had planned which is the downside for this but that's absolutely fine. Thanks as
well. You have been a guest on the show. And we have had a large number of guests. Much like the
episodes I started to put together a list of every guests and realized it was too tall of a
task. We have just had so many people on the show and it has been largely enjoyable. I know Darren
presented at the Roguelike Celebration as well. ALEXEI: I will let you in on a secret when we are
trying to figure out who to invite to Roguelike Celebration looking at who appeared on an episode
of Roguelike Radio is a handy checklist to look for inspiration for sourcing Roguelike Radio
since you have done a great job of finding people with interesting work willing to talk about it.
ANDREW: And we are back. The hiatus we had was not intentional. I am working
full time and my interest has largely moved elsewhere from roguelikes but
nothing is stopping anyone from watching this recording episode and sending it to us and say
I want to appear on the show. I have something burning to talk about. You were wrong with
what you said about Python in 2013 or whatever. ALEXEI: And you talked about your ethos of we are
all just at signs and something that's important to Roguelike Celebration and someone who has had
a lot of games that didn't ship and there is stuff as a game developer and in the roguelike community
where you have people that are knowledgeable and dedicated but don't have big name games.
It is just very hard. A lot of conferences put a lot of weight on your accolades and so I think it
is really great that Roguelike Radio and we try to do this too where we are all here because we know
interesting things and want to talk about them. ANDREW: Your number one qualification is you
played the game we want to talk about and have something to say. We don't put weight
on how you have been here forever. Or you are the first person to come on the scene
as long as you have something you want to say you are more than invited on the show.
ALEXEI: Excellent. That's coming up on time. This has been a really nice way
to end our Saturday. Thank you so much and Thank you for making the time zones work to
be able to present live. I think it is fully Sunday for you. You have a full day ahead.
ANDREW: We are in the future which is why I am working on science fiction now.
ALEXEI: Thank you so much. If you didn't know, Roguelike Radio is back. Go listen and look
through the backlog. There is just a wealth of great stuff there. Excellent. Wonderful. OK.
